course.title: AI for actual work
course.description: A free, practical course for working professionals who have tried an AI chat tool and still use it one question at a time. You bring one recurring, low-risk job from your own work and turn it into a repeatable AI-assisted workflow with written context, an explicit level of agency, checks that catch realistic errors, and a record another person can inspect. Worked illustrative cases cover a research brief, an operational handover, and a stakeholder update. Coding is not required at any point on the core path.
course.audience: Working professionals in operations, product, research, analysis, marketing, law, finance, or software. You need one recurring task you already do and access to an approved tool that can read text you give it. You do not need coding skills, admin rights, a budget for integrations, a team, or permission to automate anything that changes an external system.
course.outcome: You finish with one real recurring job running as an inspectable AI-assisted workflow, plus a set of artefacts that record what actually happened on a real run rather than what you intended to do. Where the evidence runs out, the workflow says so instead of guessing.

sections.outcome: Choose the recurring job you will carry through the whole course, clear it for real data with a permission check, and describe how two setups behave on that job without turning the description into a ranking.

The attached example is a real artefact from recent weeks rather than one reconstructed from memory.

content.text: The difference between an answer and a job

A common first trial of AI is to ask it a question. You open a chat box, type something, read the reply, and close the tab. The reply might even be good. Nothing about your actual work changed, because the work was never in the room.

A job is a different object from a question. A job has a recipient. It has a shape it must arrive in. It carries constraints you hold in your head and never write down, and it draws on inputs scattered across places a model cannot see. Someone will notice if it is wrong. When you ask an isolated question, you are testing whether the model can produce plausible sentences. When you put a job in front of it, you are testing whether your setup can supply what the job needs. Those are separate tests, and the first tells you very little about the second.

This is why the usual trial is misleading. A free tier, a default model, and a quick question is a fair test of a chat box. It is not a fair test of the claim that this technology can carry part of your workload. If you tried it, were unimpressed, and stopped there, you may have measured the wrong thing.
Pick a job that can survive a bad first draft

The job you choose should be one you already do, more than once, where a poor first attempt costs you an hour of editing rather than a customer, a colleague, or a regulator. Recurrence matters because everything you build in this course only pays back when the same shape of work comes round again. Low risk matters because you are about to let a system produce work you have not yet learnt how to check.

Reasonable candidates: the weekly summary somebody expects on a Monday, the intake form you turn into a short brief, the recurring reconciliation between two lists, the handover note you write whenever a piece of work moves to another team. Poor candidates for a first pass: anything that leaves your organisation without review, anything involving personal data about named individuals, and anything where being wrong is expensive and quiet.

If your instinct is to pick the hardest thing you do, resist it for now, but write it down. Later in the course you will deliberately raise the ambition on a task you currently believe cannot be delegated. Starting there would run two experiments at once, and you would not know which one failed.
Write the baseline before you prompt anything
Before you type a prompt, write down how the job works today. Not how it should work. How it actually works, including the parts you do from memory without noticing.
The outcome. What has to be true for this job to be finished, stated so that another person could tell whether it is.
The inputs. Every source you draw on, including the ones you never open because you already know what they say.
The constraints. Formatting rules, tone, required wording, things your recipient has complained about before, and things you know to leave out.
The recipient. Who receives it, and what they do with it next.
The completion check. How you currently decide it is good enough to send.

The completion check is often the hardest part to write, because it is usually a feeling rather than a rule. Write down whatever you actually do, even if it amounts to reading it once more and deciding it seems fine. An honest weak check is more useful than an invented strong one. You cannot improve a check you have not admitted to.

Then attach one recent, real example of the finished job. A real artefact anchors everything that follows, because it shows the shape you are actually aiming at rather than the shape you would describe if someone asked you to describe it.
Check what you are allowed to send
This is the step people skip, and it is the one that can end badly. Before any real work data goes into a model, answer three questions in writing.

Is this an approved tool for this kind of information where you work? Look for the actual policy, an approved tool list, or a written answer from whoever owns the decision. A colleague saying that everyone uses it is not an approval.

What class of data sits in your inputs? Personal data about identifiable people, commercially confidential material, client information held under contract, and anything covered by a non-disclosure agreement each carry different rules. Being unsure is a finding, not a delay.

Where does the data go once you send it, is it retained, and is it used to train anything? Your employer's answer to that question is usually what decides whether a tool is approved for a given class of data in the first place.

If any answer is unclear, do not guess and do not proceed with the real input. Take one of two routes instead. Redact: strip names, account numbers, client identifiers, and anything else that identifies a person or a deal, then run the redacted version. Or invent: build a fictional example with the same structure and the same difficulty as the real input, and run that. Either route lets you keep working while you ask the owner of the policy for a decision in writing.

Treat an unclear answer as its own result. Not enough evidence to proceed is a legitimate place to stop, and it is the same discipline you will later build into the workflow itself. Record the answer in your baseline with the date and the name of whoever gave it. Approvals change, and in a month you will not remember whether you checked or assumed.
What you will make
One file, real-task-baseline.md, covering the job you have chosen. It holds:
The job named in one sentence, and why it recurs.
Outcome, inputs, constraints, recipient, and your current completion check.
One recent real example of the finished job, redacted if the permission check calls for it.
A short data and permission note: the class of information involved, whether the tool is approved for it, who told you, and on what date.
The route you will take if the permission answer is unclear: redacted input, invented input, or paused pending a decision.

Keep it as plain text or Markdown somewhere you can open in seconds. You will read from this file in every remaining lesson, and you will amend it as the job turns out to differ from your description of it.
Try it on your work
List every recurring job you did in the last two weeks. Aim for ten. Do not filter yet.
Cross out anything that happens less often than monthly, and anything where a wrong first draft would reach a customer, a regulator, or a public channel without review.
From what remains, pick the one that annoys you most. Irritation is a decent proxy for repeated overhead.
Write the baseline for that job using the five items above. Give yourself twenty minutes, stop when the time runs out, and fill the gaps later.
Run the permission check and write the answer down, including the parts that came back unclear.
Attach one recent finished example, redacted or replaced with an invented equivalent if the permission check says so.
Hand the file to a colleague who does similar work and ask them to name one thing you left out. There will be one.
Check your work
Your baseline is doing its job when all of the following hold.
A colleague can read the outcome line and decide whether a finished piece of work meets it, without asking you what you meant.
Someone unfamiliar with the job could locate every input you listed, or the file records that they cannot and explains why.
The completion check describes something you genuinely do, rather than a process you wish you followed.
The permission note names the class of data, the approval status, and the person or document it came from.
If permission is unclear, the file says which route you are taking and who has been asked to decide.
The attached example is a real artefact from the last few weeks, not a reconstruction.

content.text: Loyalty is not literacy

People form attachments to these tools quickly, and the attachment usually forms before any real testing. Someone tries one assistant, gets a good result on a task that happened to suit it, and becomes an advocate. Someone else tries a different one on a bad day and writes off the whole category. Both are reporting a single sample, and both will defend it in a meeting.

What is worth knowing is not which tool wins. That question has no durable answer. The tools change every few months, and a ranking you write down today will be stale before you have finished acting on it. What lasts is your ability to observe how a given setup behaves on your job, and to notice quickly when it starts behaving differently. Treat the comparison as a measurement of your own workflow rather than a verdict on a product.
The comparison below is designed to produce a description of what happened. It is not a scoring exercise, and you should be suspicious of any conclusion from it that sounds like a recommendation.
Change one thing, run the same job twice

Take the job from your baseline and run it end to end twice. Between the two runs, change exactly one thing. Keep everything else identical: the same input, the same request, the same idea of what finished looks like.
The thing you change can be the tool, or it can be a configuration of the same tool. Useful variations:
Two different assistants you already have legitimate access to, both approved for this class of data.
The same assistant with and without your baseline file supplied as context.
A one-line request against a request that states the outcome, the constraints, and the recipient.
The same assistant with and without explicit permission to ask you clarifying questions before it starts.

The middle two variations are usually more informative than swapping tools, and they cost nothing. A large share of the difference people attribute to tools comes from what the tool was given to work with.
Record behaviour, not writing style
Judging the output on prose quality is the trap. Fluency is the thing these systems are best at, so it barely discriminates between setups. Record four things instead.
Questions asked. What did it stop and ask you, and at what point in the job? Write the questions down word for word.
Evidence used. Which of your inputs did it actually draw on, which did it ignore, and did anything appear in the output that you never supplied?

Failure shape. When it went wrong, what kind of wrong was it? Confidently inventing a detail is a different problem from silently dropping a section, which is different again from misreading what you asked for.
Recovery cost. What did it take to get back on track? One clarifying sentence, a rewritten request, or starting the run again?

Interrupts deserve particular attention. When a system stops to ask you something, gets a correct answer from you, and then proceeds without further trouble, the capability was already there and the knowledge was not. That often points at something living only in your head, with no path out to the place the system could read it.

Do not push that reading too far. An interrupt can also mean the request itself was ambiguous, that the task sits beyond what the system can currently do, or that it lacks the access or authority it needs and is asking you to supply it. Note which of those you believe it was, and label the note as a judgement rather than a finding.
Illustrative case: a research brief

The case below is invented for teaching. The person, the request, and the results are constructed to show what a filled-in behaviour card looks like. It is not a measured result and it is not evidence about any particular product.

A policy analyst produces a short research brief every fortnight: three to five pages summarising what changed in a regulated area, with every claim attributed to a named source. The input is a folder of documents they have already gathered. The recipient is a director who reads only the first page.

Run one supplies the folder and a one-line request to summarise the documents into a brief. The system returns five fluent pages. Two claims carry no source. One paragraph describes a consultation that appears in none of the documents. It never asks a question at any point.

Run two supplies the same folder plus the baseline file, which states the outcome, the attribution rule, the page limit, and who reads it. The system stops after reading the folder and asks which of two overlapping documents supersedes the other. The analyst answers in one sentence. The brief comes back at four pages, every claim attributed, with one section marked as not enough evidence to state a position.

The card for that pair records one interrupt in run two and none in run one, invented content as the failure shape in run one, a recovery cost of a single sentence in run two, and the observation that the only variable changed was context. The useful conclusion is about the analyst's setup. Nothing in the pair supports a durable claim about either configuration beyond this job on this day.
When it misses, decide what the miss is telling you
Watch what you do in the second after a bad result. The reflex is usually one of two.

The first treats the miss as a verdict: this does not work, so I will do it myself. It feels decisive. It teaches you nothing, and it leaves you doing by hand a piece of work that will come round again next month.

The second treats the miss as a report against your own setup: I have not taught it this yet. That opens a move the first reflex cannot see, which is to change the thing that does the work instead of doing the work.

The second reflex has its own failure, and it is an expensive one. You can spend an afternoon improving a setup for a task the system genuinely cannot do yet, and ship something worse than what you would have written by hand in the first hour. So apply a filter at the moment of the miss. Ask whether this is a general gap that will recur, in which case improving the setup is worth doing and should be given a time limit, or the current ceiling on this specific thing, in which case do it by hand now and log the gap to revisit later.
Keep the delivery and the experiment apart. A piece of work with a deadline on it should not quietly become your research project.
What you will make
One file, tool-behaviour-card.md, holding:
The job you ran, and the single thing you changed between run one and run two.
For each run: questions asked, evidence used and ignored, failure shape, and recovery cost.
Your reading of each interrupt: missing written context, ambiguous request, missing access or authority, or a current ceiling. Marked as a judgement.
One belief about this job that the runs changed, or a note that neither run shifted anything you believed.
A review date. Anything you conclude here has a short shelf life.
Try it on your work
Confirm both setups are approved for the class of data named in your baseline. If either is not, use the redacted or invented input from the previous lesson for both runs.
Fix the input and the request in writing before you start, so the second run cannot quietly drift.
Run one. Record the four observations as they happen, not afterwards from memory.
Change exactly one thing. Run two. Record the same four observations.
Classify every interrupt across both runs using the four causes above.
Pick one belief you hold about this job, such as the idea that it cannot be delegated because the tone has to be yours, and design a small run that could prove you wrong. Run it.
Write the card and put a review date on it before you close the file.
Check your work
The card names one changed variable, and a reader can tell what stayed the same.
Every interrupt is recorded with the actual wording of the question.
At least one failure is described by its shape rather than by how bad it felt.
The card contains no claim that one tool is better than another, only what each did on this job on this day.
Every conclusion is dated and carries a trigger for reviewing it.
If you tested a belief about the job, the card says what would have proved you wrong, and whether it did.
A card that concludes one setup is simply better has almost certainly measured writing style. Go back to the questions asked and the failure shapes, because that is where setups actually differ.

technicalExtension.title: Optional lab: measure your tool surface against your context budget
technicalExtension.outcome: Measure what your agent harness costs in context before a task starts, then decide per integration whether a declared tool schema or an on demand script is the better trade this month.

content.text: Why this is optional

Nothing on the core path needs a terminal, and skipping this changes nothing in the sections that follow. This lab is for readers who already run a coding agent against a repository and would rather measure the harness than argue about it.
The trade you are actually making

A tool integration that declares its full schema at startup pays a fixed context cost in every session, whether or not the task ever touches it. A script the agent invokes on demand costs nothing until it runs, at the price of the agent having to discover that it exists and what flags it takes. Neither arrangement is permanently correct. Which one wins depends on how large the schema is, how often the tool is genuinely called, and how much context the model you are running has to spare. All three of those move with every release, so treat any conclusion here as a measurement rather than a rule.
Measure before deciding
Open a session with your full tool surface loaded and record the context consumed before you send a single task.
Open a second session with the integrations you rarely use removed, and record the same number.

Divide the difference by how often those integrations were actually called across a week of real work. If you paid for them in every session and called them twice, you have your candidate for conversion.
The conversion target is a script the agent can discover and call, with a help flag that describes its own interface. The shape, using your own binary and identifiers:

# discoverable on demand, costs context only when called
./scripts/fetch-record --help
./scripts/fetch-record ABC-123 --format json

Two properties fall out of this that a static declaration cannot offer. The agent decides at run time which scripts to pull in, so nothing has to be declared up front. And when a script does not quite fit the task, the agent can edit it, because it is only code.
Keep the conclusion dated

Write the decision down with the date, the model and context size you measured against, and the call frequency you used. Revisit it when any of those change. A verdict of this kind is a measurement of one month, and treating it as a standing rule is how teams end up carrying a harness that suited a model they stopped running some time ago.

content.text: The answer you gave today will be wanted again

In the last lesson you recorded the questions a system stopped to ask you. Each of those was a moment where the work paused, you supplied something from your own head, and the work resumed. The answer solved that instance. Next week the same gap opens and you answer it again, slightly differently, and nothing has accumulated.
The move that changes this is small. When you answer, do not only answer. Write down the rule your answer came from, and write down why the rule exists.

Take a question like whether a weekly summary should include pending items that have nobody assigned to them. The thin answer is yes. The rule is that unowned items go in under their own heading, because the person reading this uses it to chase owners, and the unowned ones are the whole reason the summary is sent. The thin answer covers one summary. The rule covers every summary, and it also covers cases nobody has thought of yet, because a reader who knows the reason can work out what to do with an item that is half owned.

The reason is the load-bearing part, and it is the part people leave out. A rule without its reason cannot be stretched to a case it does not literally describe, and worse, it cannot be retired. When the reason stops being true, a bare instruction just sits there being obeyed.
Keep an interrupt log for one working day

One day is enough. Longer and you will stop recording honestly. For each interrupt write down when it happened, what you were doing, the exact wording of the question, the answer you gave, the rule behind the answer, and the reason.

Then add the interrupts that never appeared as questions. Every time you edit the output in the same way you edited it last time, that is an interrupt you performed silently. Cutting the same opening paragraph, reordering the same section, restoring the same wording that legal insists on. These are usually the most valuable entries in the log, because nobody ever asked you about them and so nothing ever prompted you to write them down.
Write rules that can be checked
Give every rule four parts: the situation it applies to, the behaviour it requires, the reason it exists, and how you would tell whether it had been followed.
That fourth part is what stops a rules file filling up with wishes. Rules that fail this test are easy to spot once you look for them:
Tone instructions with no observable outcome. Asking for a professional register gives you nothing to check against.
Rules that restate what any competent reader would already do. They cost attention on every run and change nothing.
Rules that contradict another rule you wrote three weeks ago and have not reread since.
Rules describing something the system could work out from the input in front of it.

Store the rules close enough to the work that the system actually reads them. A rule in your head is not a rule. A rule in a document nobody attaches to the run is not a rule either. If the tool takes a file, put them in a file and attach it. If it takes a persistent instruction, put them there. The test is mechanical: does the next run see them without you remembering to paste anything?
Verify that the interrupt actually stopped
Writing the rule is not the result. The result is that the same question stops being asked. Run the job again with the rules supplied and count the interrupts against your log.

When one recurs, there are two different faults and they need different repairs. Either the rule was never reached, or it was reached and did not settle anything. Tell them apart by asking the system which rule it applied and why. If it cannot name the rule, the storage or the routing is broken, and no amount of rewording will help. If it names the rule and still did something else, the rule is ambiguous or it collides with another one, and the fix is in the wording.
Keep the recurrences in the log with the diagnosis attached. That record is what tells you, in a month, whether your rules file is getting better or just getting longer.
Why this is worth the effort

Most knowledge work evaporates. You spend an hour on a careful reply that captures your current thinking, and it ends up in a sent folder and in the fading impression it left on two people. Andy Matuschak makes this point in a note called Knowledge Work Should Accrete, and quotes Soenke Ahrens on the same idea: without a permanent reservoir, you are limited to the length of one project or the capacity of your memory.

A day of answering the same questions is exactly that kind of evaporating effort. The rules file is the reservoir. It is a modest one, and it will not transform your week, but it is the difference between a year of explaining the same constraint and a file that explains it for you.
What you will make
interrupt-log.md, covering one full working day, with both the questions asked and the corrections you made silently.
working-rules.md, holding at least five rules, each with situation, behaviour, reason and check.
A note at the end of the log recording which interrupts stopped after the rules were supplied, and the diagnosis for any that recurred.
Try it on your work
Pick a working day and keep the log open beside the work. Record interrupts as they happen.
At each interrupt, answer the question, then write the rule and the reason before you carry on. It takes about a minute and it will not survive being deferred to the evening.
At the end of the day, reread the output you produced and add every correction you made out of habit.
Write the five strongest rules into working-rules.md with all four parts. Discard anything you cannot write a check for.
Attach the rules to the next run and do the job again on a fresh instance.
Count the interrupts. For each one that recurred, ask which rule was applied, and record whether the rule was unreachable or unclear.
Repair the wording or the storage, whichever the diagnosis pointed at, and leave the old version in the file marked as replaced.
Check your work
Every rule carries its reason, and the reason explains something a reader could not guess.
Every rule has a check you could apply to a finished piece of work without asking the author what they intended.
At least one rule came from a silent correction rather than from a question.
The rules were read by the second run without you pasting anything by hand.
The log records the second run honestly, including interrupts that came back.
Nothing in the file is a rule you would be unable to defend if a colleague asked why it is there.

content.text: One big instruction file is the wrong shape

Rules files grow. Yours will too. The usual path is that everything useful gets pasted into one document, the document reaches eleven pages, and two things go wrong at once. The system spends its attention reading a map of your work instead of doing the work, and the middle of the document quietly goes stale because nobody scrolls that far.

The better shape is a router. A short file that is always in play, holding the constraints that matter on nearly every run, plus pointers to where the real detail lives. Shortness is a side effect rather than the goal: a very short file that hides the important paths is no better than a long one.
Four kinds of context, four different homes
Sort every line you have written into one of four buckets.
Always-on constraints. Needed on nearly every run, high impact, and impossible to work out from the inputs. These stay in the router. Aim for a handful of lines.
Task procedure. The steps for one class of work. Loaded when that work comes up and ignored otherwise.
Durable explanation. Why the work is shaped this way, which decisions are still live, what must not change. Read when somebody needs the reasoning, including you in six months.
Source evidence. The raw material: the live queue, the signed contract, the meeting transcript, the current policy. These are inputs, not context.

That last distinction catches people out. A folder of evidence is not context just because it is available. It becomes context when somebody has curated the part that matters and put it somewhere the run will read. Until then it is a pile you are hoping will be searched well.

For the router itself, use a two-question filter on every line. Is this needed on almost every run? Can it be worked out from the source, the input, or the procedure it belongs to? If the first answer is no, move it out. If the second answer is yes, delete it and point at the real source instead.
Documentation is a lead, not the truth

Anything written down is a snapshot of the moment somebody wrote it. Specifications drift. Decisions get reversed in practice without anyone updating the page that described them. A document tells you where to look. The live thing tells you what is true today.

For work that is not code, the live thing is the current policy, the signed agreement, the system of record, the spreadsheet people actually update. When it disagrees with your written description, the live source wins on what is true now. The description may still be the only record of why the arrangement was set up that way, so mark it as superseded and point at the replacement rather than deleting the reasoning. Losing the reasoning is how a team relitigates the same decision every year.
Illustrative case: an operational handover

This case is invented for teaching. The team, the document and the outcome are constructed to show what routing and maintenance look like when they are done. It is not a measured result and it is not drawn from any real organisation.

A support team hands its open case queue to an on-call group every Friday. The operational handover note has to say what is open, what is blocked, who owns each item, and what is likely to break over the weekend. The instructions for producing it had grown to eleven pages over about a year.

The split came out like this. Three always-on constraints: never name a customer in the note, always state an owner or write the word unowned, never mark an item closed without a reference. The Friday steps became task procedure, loaded only on Fridays. The explanation of why unowned items are escalated, which dates from an incident two years earlier, became durable explanation. The live case queue and the on-call rota were reclassified as source evidence, to be read at run time rather than summarised into the document.

The behaviour that changed most was owner attribution. The old document contained a paragraph describing who tended to own which area, which had been true when it was written. The system had been reading that paragraph and inferring owners from it. Once the procedure said to read the rota instead, the invented owners stopped.

Then the maintenance. The escalation explanation is reviewed when the incident policy changes, and the incident owner is named in the table. The rota pointer is checked whenever the rota moves, which is monthly. The always-on constraints are reviewed whenever somebody proposes a fourth one, because that is the moment the file is at risk of becoming a handbook again.
Every durable item needs an update trigger

Once you write something down and let a system read it, you have taken on the job of keeping it current. Written context that nobody maintains does not stay neutral. It becomes a confident, out of date instruction that a system will follow.

A field that nobody ever updates is the clearest version of this. Mark a page as active, finish the work, walk away, and the marker stays active forever. It looked like a queryable status and it turned into noise. Any label without a maintenance trigger behaves the same way: it is decoration rather than memory.

Prefer triggers that fire on an event rather than on a date. Reviewing something when the rota changes is a consequence of the world moving. Reviewing something quarterly is a promise, and promises about documentation are usually broken quietly. Where no event exists, a date is the honest answer, so use one and write it in the file rather than in your head.

It helps to see this as a lifecycle rather than a filing problem. A piece of written context gets created, shaped, maintained, retrieved, used, and eventually revised or retired. Most attention goes to creating and retrieving. The stage that decides whether the whole thing is worth anything is the maintenance in the middle, which is exactly the stage with no deadline attached to it.

One more distinction that stops arguments. Sumers and colleagues, writing on cognitive architectures for language agents in 2023, separate what a system holds right now, what it remembers happening, what it holds as true, and how it knows to act. Those are four different problems. When someone says a system needs more context, ask which one they mean: a bigger working view of the task, a record of what happened last time, a durable fact that is missing, or a procedure that was never written. Each has a different fix, and treating them as one thing is why instruction files grow.
What you will make
context-router.md, holding the always-on constraints and pointers to everything else.
Separate files or sections for task procedure and durable explanation, reachable from the router.
context-maintenance-table.md, listing every durable item with its update trigger and its owner.
A short record of the one documentation claim you checked against the live source, and what you found.
Try it on your work
Open your longest instruction document and label every line with one of the four buckets. Do not edit yet, just label.
Apply the two-question filter to everything you labelled as always-on. Most lines will fail it. Move or delete them.
Delete anything the system could work out from the input in front of it, and replace it with a pointer to that input.
Move procedure into its own place, loaded only for the class of work it serves.
Pick the oldest claim in your durable explanation and check it against the live source. Record whether it still holds. If it does not, mark it superseded and write the current truth beside it.
Build the maintenance table. For each durable item, name the event that should trigger a review and the person who owns it. Write unowned where that is the honest answer.
Run the job once with the router in place and confirm nothing you removed turned out to be load bearing. Restore anything that was, in the bucket it actually belongs to.
Check your work
Someone could read the router in under a minute and know where everything else lives.
Every line left in the router survives both filter questions, and you could say which run last needed it.
No line in the router describes something the system could read directly from the input.
Every durable item has a trigger, and the trigger names an event or a date rather than an intention.
Every durable item names an owner, or is explicitly marked unowned so the gap is visible.
The claim you checked has a written result, including the case where it turned out to be stale.
Superseded reasoning is marked and kept, not deleted.

If your maintenance table has more rows than your router has lines, that is usually correct. The router is meant to be small. The durable material behind it is where the substance sits, and it is the part that rots if nobody is named against it.

technicalExtension.title: Optional lab: audit repository instructions and regenerate a reference surface
technicalExtension.outcome: Apply the two-question filter to a repository's always-on instruction file, move procedural depth into scoped modules, and regenerate one reference surface from source so the build fails when the two disagree.
sourceNotes: Always-On Agent Context Is a Router.md

content.text: Why this is optional

The core path already taught the routing idea. This lab applies it to a repository, where the instruction file has a name, the evidence is code, and the update trigger can be a build failure rather than a promise. Skipping it changes nothing in the next section.
Audit the always-on file

Open your repository's AGENTS.md and put every line through the same two questions. Is it needed on almost every task? Is it undiscoverable from code, config or tooling? Package manifests, test configuration, lint rules and folder structure all fail the second question, so delete them outright. Topic-specific workflows that only matter sometimes move into a scoped skill or module. What stays is a short list of global, high-impact constraints plus the routing table that says which module to load for which class of work.

Expect the file to shrink hard, and expect almost nothing to be lost. Architecture boundaries usually already live in architecture docs and manifests. Command surfaces usually already live in generated reference. An overgrown instruction file is mostly a duplicate of things with better homes, and the duplicate is the copy that goes stale.
Generate the reference and fail on drift
Pick one mechanical surface where a type, schema or help output is the canonical declaration. Generate the reference page from it, then make disagreement a build error rather than a review comment.

# regenerate, then fail the build if the committed page drifted
npm run docs:generate
git diff --exit-code docs/reference

# run the documented command from the directory the page names
cd packages/cli && ./bin/tool --help

That second command matters more than it looks. A command example is an executable contract, and the working directory is part of it. Reference generation will not catch a path that resolves differently from where the page tells the reader to stand.
Know what generation cannot defend

Generated pages protect flags, schemas and routes. They do not protect hand-written explanation, glossaries, navigation, or packaging promises, and they will faithfully reproduce a stale help string if the source text was never updated. They also do not help when the generator's own manifest lists fewer pages than the command tree, which is a quieter kind of rot: the defence exists and is checking the wrong set.

Finally, if the repository commits generated agent context so that a fresh clone works immediately, those committed files are a generated surface too. They need a job that reruns the installer when the upstream package moves and commits the refreshed output. Without that loop, committed context is just stale context with a better name.

sections.title: Choose the mechanism before the prompt
sections.outcome: Place your recurring job on the ladder of policy, workflow and agent, argue it down a rung wherever you can, and check that the process underneath could support the promise before any model is added to it.

lessons.title: Use policy, workflow or agent on purpose
lessons.outcome: Place ten real tasks on the ladder of policy, workflow and agent, defend each placement against somebody arguing it down a rung, and decide who approves a promotion.
lessons.exercise: List ten tasks you actually did this month and place each on the ladder. Ask a colleague to argue every one of them down a rung, and record which arguments held. For any task that moved, write what changed your mind. For any that did not, write what would have to become true for it to move later.

artifact.description: A record of ten real tasks with the rung each sits on, the argument for the rung below, whether that argument held, and the condition that would let the task move down later, plus a note on who approves a promotion and what evidence they would want.

verification: Every task names its rung and gives the reason that rung is the lowest one that can do the job.
Each task carries a real argument for the rung below, written by someone other than you where possible.
At least one task moved down a rung, or the record explains why none of them could.
Tasks that stayed high name the specific condition that would let them move down later.
The record names who approves a promotion and what evidence that person would need to see.

content.text: Three ways to allocate judgement
A common first move is to write a prompt. The more useful first question is how much judgement this job actually needs to hand over. There are three answers, and they form a ladder.
A policy decides how known facts produce an outcome. Reach for it when the people who know the work can state the rules in advance.
A workflow decides which known steps gather the facts or carry out the action. Reach for it when the route repeats, even if one step inside it uses a model.
An agent decides what to investigate and which route to take. Reach for it when the route genuinely cannot be known in advance.

Start at the lowest rung that can solve the problem. A policy is easier to test than a workflow, because you can feed it cases and check the answers. A workflow is easier to replay than an agent choosing its own path, because the path is the same one you wrote down. Every rung you climb buys flexibility and costs you the ability to explain what happened.
Keep the boundaries clean

A policy answers a question and changes nothing. May this go out? Which band does this fall into? Is this wording within what we have approved? It is declarative, and it has no side effects, which is exactly why it is cheap to test.

A workflow gathers inputs and acts on the answer. It might pull the figures, look up the approved wording, ask you for a missing date, apply the policy, then send or escalate depending on what came back.
An agent is what you reach for when nobody can say in advance which of those steps will be needed, or in what order.

A policy should not have to become a workflow before it can run. Keep it separable: a workflow can call it and branch on the result, and an agent can call the same one. That way the decision rules have a single home and one version, rather than three slightly different copies in three places.

One thing to avoid. Do not hide the decision rules inside the wording of a prompt. Instructions to a model get reinterpreted, and the reinterpretation is invisible until it produces a wrong answer that reads well. Keep the rules somewhere a person can read them, in language that means the same thing on every run.
Argue every task down a rung

Placing tasks on the ladder alone is too easy, because your first instinct will usually be one rung too high. The useful version is adversarial. Write your placements down, then get somebody who knows the work to argue every task down a rung and make you defend it.

Two collapses come up again and again. A task labelled agent turns out to be a workflow the moment you write down what you actually did the last three times, because you did the same thing all three times and only felt like you were improvising. A task labelled workflow turns out to be a policy when the only real variable is which band something falls into, and everything around that is fetching and formatting.

Some tasks survive the argument, and that is a result too. Work where the inputs arrive in a different shape every time, or where you do not know what you are looking for until you have looked, belongs higher up. Write down which argument failed and why, because that reason is the thing you will check again in six months when the inputs have settled down.
Promotion, and who approves it

The ladder is not a one-off sorting exercise. Work moves down it over time, and the movement is the point. Use an agent for genuinely novel work. Watch what it does. When the same route keeps working, that route is a candidate for a workflow. When a decision inside that workflow can be stated as facts and rules, it is a candidate for a policy.

A system can draft the workflow or the rules for you, and drafting is genuinely useful. A person approves the promotion. Automatic drafting is a saving. Automatic activation is a way to discover, some weeks later, that a rule you never read has been deciding things.

This is also the sensible place for approval in general. Approving every individual run is slow and teaches nobody anything. Writing the constraints down once, then reviewing when a constraint is being pushed or broken, keeps the attention where the risk actually is. Decide now who that reviewer is for your job, and what they would want to see before they agreed to move something down a rung.
What you will make
mechanism-decision-record.md, listing ten real tasks from the last month with the rung each sits on.
For each task, the argument for the rung below and whether it held.
For each task that stayed high, the condition that would let it move down later.
A short promotion note: who approves a move down the ladder, and what evidence they would want.
Try it on your work
List ten tasks you actually did this month. Use real ones, including the dull ones, not a list of things you would like to automate.
Place each on the ladder and write one sentence saying why that rung is the lowest that can do the job.
For anything you called an agent task, write down what you actually did the last three times you performed it. Compare the three.
Hand the list to a colleague and ask them to argue every task down one rung. Do not defend your placements while they are talking.
Record which arguments held and move those tasks. Record which failed and why.
Take the job from your baseline and write the decision rules it contains as plain sentences, separate from any prompt. If you cannot, that is evidence the job is not yet policy.
Name the person who would approve a promotion, and write down what they would need to see. If that person is you, say so, and say what would make you refuse.
Check your work
Every task names its rung and the reason that rung is the lowest one that works.
Each argument for the rung below is written out, not just recorded as won or lost.
At least one task moved down, or the record says plainly why none could.
Anything left on the agent rung names what is genuinely unknown about its route.
Any decision rules you extracted live outside the prompt and read the same way to another person.
The promotion note names a person and the evidence they would want, not a general intention to review.

lessons.title: Audit the substrate before adding AI
lessons.outcome: Check whether the process beneath your job holds the facts, timing, intent, evidence and privacy boundary that would make an AI-assisted answer true, then decide what the process does when the model cannot run.
lessons.exercise: Run the seven-part audit on the process underneath your chosen job and answer each part with ready or not yet, citing what you looked at. List every not yet as prerequisite work. Then split the job into the parts an exact method could answer and the parts that genuinely need a model, and write down what the process produces when the model is unavailable.

artifact.description: An audit of the non-AI process beneath your job answering each of the seven checks with ready or not yet and the evidence you looked at, a prerequisite list built from every not yet, the split between exact work and model work, and the written behaviour for a run where the model cannot be used.

verification: Each of the seven checks has a ready or not yet answer and names what you actually inspected.
Every not yet appears in the prerequisite list as work to do before the AI step, not as a caveat.
The split says which parts a lookup, filter or checklist could answer without a model.
The model-disabled behaviour is written down and produces either a bounded useful result or an explicit failure.
No part of the audit assumes a field is populated without you having opened it and looked.

content.text: A model can hide a hole in the process

A model will produce a plausible answer even when the process underneath never captured the fact that would make the answer trustworthy. That is the dangerous kind of clever. The demonstration works, everybody is impressed, and the underlying process is exactly as weak as it was before.

So before adding AI to a step, ask a different question. Not whether a model could do this, because the answer is nearly always yes. Ask whether the process has the facts, the timing, the recorded intent, the evidence, the privacy boundary and the consistency that would make the output true.
The seven checks
Answer each one with ready or not yet, and name what you looked at to decide.
Truth of the data. Are the fields you would rely on actually filled in by the current process, or are they placeholders somebody intended to populate?
Lifecycle point. Is there a place where a check could run before anything irreversible happens: before it is sent, before it is filed, before the payment leaves?
Captured intent. Does the process record what the person meant, or would you be inferring it later from weak signals?
Evidence shape. Can the output point at the specific row, paragraph, message or document behind each claim, or only gesture at a folder?
Privacy boundary. Does the step apply the data rules before anything is assembled and sent, rather than relying on someone noticing afterwards?
Shared behaviour. Do all the routes into this work behave the same way, or does the person using the spreadsheet get a different answer from the person using the form?
Documentation truth. Does the written description match what the process does now, rather than the plan that used to be true?

Every not yet is prerequisite work. It is not a caveat to note and move past. The AI step is the last mile, and the boring process underneath is the part that decides whether the last mile means anything.
Do the cheap exact work first

If a lookup, a filter, a sorted list, a checklist or a simple calculation can answer part of the job, use that. The model runs where the exact method cannot answer, rather than first because it is the interesting option.

This is restraint, not scepticism. Exact methods fail the same way every time, so you can trace what happened and repair it. Model steps fail differently on each run, which means a bug you saw yesterday may not reproduce today. Given a choice between two things that work, take the one whose failures you can read.

The model earns its place on genuine synthesis, on judgement under uncertainty, on turning unstructured prose into something structured, and where an exact method exists but produces so many false alarms that nobody reads them. It is the wrong tool when a lookup would answer it, when it would fire on every single item, when its output causes a side effect with nobody reviewing, and when the main reason for reaching for it is that the result feels more advanced.
Decide what happens when the model cannot run

One day the tool will be down, out of quota, or not approved for the data in front of you. Decide now what the process does then, and write it into the design rather than discovering it under pressure.

Two answers are acceptable. Either the exact path still produces a useful bounded result, clearly marked as incomplete, or the process stops and says plainly that this step could not run. What is not acceptable is quiet degradation that looks like success, because then nobody ever learns the model mattered, and the first time anybody finds out is when a wrong answer has already been acted on.
Illustrative case: a monthly stakeholder update

This case is invented for teaching. The programme, the partners and the findings are constructed to show what a completed audit looks like. It is not a measured result and it does not describe any real organisation.

A programme manager sends a monthly stakeholder update to a board of five external partners. It reports which commitments were met, which slipped and why, how spending compares with plan, and what the partners need to decide before the next meeting. Somebody proposes generating the whole thing from the project tracker.

The audit came back mostly not yet. On truth of the data, the slip dates are maintained for two of the four workstreams; the other two still carry their original dates because nobody updates them once a date moves. On lifecycle, there is a good point to check a draft, the Friday before the Monday send, so that one is ready. On captured intent, the tracker records that a date changed but never why it changed, and the reason is precisely what the update has to say. On evidence, every commitment carries an identifier, so a claim can point at a specific row, which is ready.

The last three are where it gets serious. On the privacy boundary, two of the five partners are contractually barred from seeing a third partner's figures, and nothing in the process enforces that. It lives in the manager's memory. On shared behaviour, three workstreams report through the tracker and one reports by email, so the fourth would simply be invisible in anything generated from the tracker. On documentation truth, the written process still describes a fortnightly cadence that changed a year ago.

So the AI step is not the first job. The prerequisites are a field for the reason a date moved, a visibility rule that lives outside one person's head, and getting the fourth workstream to report where the others do. None of that is exciting and all of it is the actual work.

What survives the audit is a much narrower role for the model. Turn the changed rows into readable prose in the register the board expects, and flag any commitment where the reason is missing instead of writing smoothly around the gap. Everything else, which commitments changed, what the spend figures are, who may see what, is a lookup and a rule. And the disabled behaviour is written down: if the model cannot run, the process still produces the table of commitments and slips from the tracker, marked as awaiting prose, and the manager writes the paragraphs. The update goes out late rather than wrong.
What you will make
substrate-audit.md, with each of the seven checks answered ready or not yet and the evidence you looked at.
A prerequisite list built from every not yet, ordered by what blocks the most.
The split between the parts an exact method can answer and the narrow part that needs a model.
The written behaviour for a run where the model is unavailable or not approved for the data.
Try it on your work
Take the job from your baseline and write down the non-AI process underneath it as it runs today, including the manual steps.
Work through the seven checks in order. For truth of the data, open the actual records and look at whether the fields are filled in. Do not answer from memory.
For captured intent, find one recent case and try to reconstruct why a decision was made using only what the process recorded. If you cannot, that check is not yet.
For the privacy boundary, name where the rule is enforced. If the answer is that somebody remembers, write that down plainly.
Turn every not yet into a prerequisite with an owner, and decide whether you can proceed on a reduced version of the job in the meantime.
Split the job. Write two lists: what a lookup, filter or checklist could answer, and what genuinely needs synthesis or judgement.
Write the model-disabled behaviour as a short paragraph, then test it by doing one run without the model and seeing whether the result is honest.
Check your work
Every check names the thing you inspected, not the thing you assumed was true.
At least one check came back not yet, or you can explain why a process this clean has not been automated already.
Every not yet has an owner and sits in the prerequisite list rather than in a paragraph of caveats.
The exact-work list is longer than you expected when you started, which is the usual outcome.
The model-disabled run was actually performed once, and the result was honest rather than quietly incomplete.
The remaining role for the model is narrow enough to describe in one sentence.

technicalExtension.title: Optional lab: map evidence to a fact ledger, policy and trace
technicalExtension.outcome: Lay out one governed path from unstructured input through evidence resolvers, an append-only fact ledger, a versioned pure policy and a decision trace, to a workflow action, and know which two guarantees the layout does not give you.

content.text: Why this is optional
The core lessons taught the ladder and the audit as judgement. This lab is the implementation shape for people building the system, and nothing in the next section depends on it.
The shape

unstructured input
  -> evidence resolvers (queries, parsers, retrieval, model, human review)
  -> append-only fact ledger
  -> versioned policy -> decision trace
  -> workflow action, clarification, review, or refusal
  -> agent only where the route is still genuinely open
What each layer owns

Resolvers turn unstructured input into atomic facts. A model can sit here as a bounded sensor that resolves one small fact at a time, which is a very different job from letting it own the decision. That is what makes deterministic architecture usable even when the raw input is prose: the question stops being rules or model, and becomes which facts need language interpretation and which decisions can stay policy.

The ledger is append only. Facts get superseded rather than overwritten, so a decision taken last month can still be replayed against what was known at the time. The policy is versioned and pure: no clock read, no database call, no model call inside it. Purity is what turns a replayable trace from an aspiration into a property you get for free. The trace records the policy version, every fact with the resolver that produced it, the facts that were missing or in conflict, the intermediate results, and the outcome. The workflow then acts on that outcome by performing, clarifying, escalating or refusing.
Two things this does not buy you

A structured decision object can be internally consistent while the prose printed beside it says something else. Structured output guarantees shape, not agreement, and closing that gap needs a language judgement, which belongs in monitoring rather than in a gate. Separately, a citation proves the source existed and was reachable. It never proves the source supports the claim. Name that residual in a comment next to the check, because the next reader will assume the check covers more than it does.
Roll it out in shadow first

A policy layer's real false-alarm rate is not knowable from fixtures. Run the first version recording only, compare its verdicts against what humans actually decided, and enforce once the disagreements are understood. That also gives promotion a data-driven trigger instead of a feeling. Give the policy its own regression fixtures stating what the rule should decide, kept separate from any evaluation of the model, because those fixtures catch ordering and precedence bugs that no amount of model evaluation will surface.

sections.title: Build checks that can prove you wrong
sections.outcome: Write checks that come from what the work has to achieve rather than from what the system produced last time, then order your workflow so the checks that can fail cheaply run before anything expensive or irreversible.

lessons.title: Derive expectations from the requirement
lessons.outcome: Write a check for one recurring deliverable that comes from what the work must achieve rather than from a previous output, then prove it fails by deliberately producing a plausible wrong result.
lessons.exercise: Take one recurring deliverable and write down what the recipient actually requires. Write the check you would naturally reach for first, then describe a plausible wrong result that would sail past it. Repair the check so it catches that result, then break the work on purpose and record what the repaired check reported.

artifact.description: A file holding the requirement in the recipient's terms, the weak first check, a plausible wrong result that the weak check would pass, the repaired check, and the recorded evidence from a deliberate breakage showing the repaired check failed for the right reason.

verification: The requirement is written in terms of what the recipient needs, not in terms of the steps you take.
The plausible wrong result is one that could genuinely happen, not an empty or obviously broken output.
The repaired check compares against the requirement rather than against a previous output.
You produced a deliberately wrong result and recorded what the repaired check actually reported.
The recorded failure names the reason, so a reader can tell the check failed for the right cause.

content.text: Where expected results come from

There is a comfortable way to write a check and it is almost always wrong. You run the job, look at what came out, decide it seems about right, and enshrine that as the standard. From then on the check confirms whatever the system produces. It will keep confirming it long after the output has drifted away from what the work actually needed, because the output is both the thing being tested and the thing it is tested against.

Expected results come from the requirement. What did the recipient ask for? What has to be true before this is usable? Write those down before you look at a single output, and you will find the check writes itself.
A check that passes when the work is wrong is worse than having no check, because it teaches you to trust the process. That is the whole reason this lesson exists.
Five questions before a check earns its place
Would this fail on a realistic mistake? A swapped figure, a missing section, a date carried over from last month. Catching only the case where somebody deleted everything is not enough.
Do the expected values come from the requirement rather than from a previous output?
Does it cover the boundaries and the failure paths, or only the run where everything was present and tidy?
Would it still pass if somebody reorganised how the work gets done but produced the same result? A check tied to your internal steps breaks on harmless change and protects nothing.
If you deliberately break the work, does the check fail, and does it fail for the right reason?

Two weak shapes fail these questions constantly. Existence checks, which confirm that a section is present or a file is not empty, only fire when something has been removed wholesale. Snapshot checks, which compare against last month's version, take their expected value from whatever was produced rather than from what should be produced. Both feel like coverage and neither has teeth.
Three worked repairs

The three cases below are invented for teaching. The documents, the teams and the figures are constructed to show the shape of a repair. They are not drawn from real work and they are not measured results.

Start with a research brief. The requirement is that every factual claim is attributable to a named source in the supplied folder, the brief runs to no more than four pages, and anything the folder cannot settle is marked as not enough evidence rather than quietly dropped. The weak check is that the brief has a sources list. The plausible wrong result it misses is a brief with a tidy sources list where one paragraph describes a consultation that appears in none of the documents, and two claims cite a source that never mentions them. The repaired check takes every sentence stating a fact, opens the cited document, and looks for the supporting passage. Sentences with no citation and citations with no supporting passage both have to be zero, and open questions have to appear under their own heading. To prove the repair, insert one invented claim with a plausible citation into a finished brief and rerun the check. If it passes, the check is still only inspecting shape.

Next, an operational handover. The requirement is that every open item names an owner or is explicitly marked unowned, every blocked item names what it is blocked on, and nothing closed during the week appears as open. The weak check is that the handover lists all the open items. The wrong result it misses is a complete list where three items carry owners who left the team last month, and one item closed on Wednesday still shows as open because the note was assembled from an export taken on Tuesday. The repaired check confirms each named owner against the current rota, and confirms each item's status in the live system at the moment the note is produced rather than in the copy it was written from. Anything that cannot be confirmed is written on the note as unconfirmed. To prove it, take a previous week's handover, change one item's status in the live system, regenerate, and see whether the mismatch is caught.

Finally, a stakeholder communication. The requirement is that every figure reconciles with the finance system exactly, every number that changed since the last update is called out with the reason it moved, and nothing appears that a given recipient is not entitled to see. The weak check is that the update contains a figures table. The wrong result it misses is a table that is internally consistent, adds up correctly, and contains one line carried over unchanged from last month because the source cell was blank this time. The repaired check reconciles each figure against the source and records the pair, and treats any figure identical to last month's as suspect until it is confirmed as genuinely unchanged rather than missing. To prove it, blank one source cell in a copy of the inputs, regenerate, and confirm the carried figure is flagged.
The same move runs through all three. The weak check asks whether something exists. The repaired check asks whether it is true, and names how you would know.
Break it on purpose

This is the step people skip, and skipping it is what leaves a suite of checks that have never once fired. A check you have never seen fail is a check you have never tested. Produce a wrong result deliberately, run the check, and confirm both that it fails and that what it says about the failure would help somebody fix it.

Predict before you run. Say out loud what you expect the check to report, then run it. When the prediction and the result disagree, that gap is the most useful thing you will learn all week, because it means your model of the check was wrong and you would have trusted it.

Label the deliberate breakages clearly wherever you record them. A failure that was engineered on purpose looks identical, six months later, to one that happened by accident, and somebody will waste an afternoon on it.
Why you keep doing this part yourself

Producing the work has become cheap. Knowing what to ask for, and noticing when what comes back is drifting away from it, has not. Those two skills are what let you direct any of this, and both of them rest on understanding the requirement well enough to state it precisely. Writing checks is that understanding made concrete and testable, which is why it is worth spending your own time on even when the drafting is delegated.
What you will make
check-with-teeth.md, opening with the requirement stated in the recipient's terms.
The weak check you would have written first, kept in the file rather than deleted.
A plausible wrong result that the weak check would have passed.
The repaired check, and the recorded output of the deliberate breakage that made it fail.
Try it on your work
Pick one recurring deliverable from your baseline job. Write what the recipient requires without looking at any past output.
Write the first check that comes to mind. Do not improve it yet.
Now describe a wrong result that would pass it. Make it plausible: something a rushed person or a fluent system would actually produce, not an empty file.
Repair the check so it catches that result, then run the five questions over the repaired version.
Take a real finished piece of work, introduce the wrong result into a copy of it, and predict what the check will say.
Run the check on the broken copy. Record what it reported, including the wording, and compare that with your prediction.
Run the check once on genuinely correct work to confirm it passes. A check that fails on everything is no more useful than one that passes on everything.
Check your work
The requirement is written in the recipient's terms and never mentions how you produce the work.
No expected value in the check was copied from something the system produced earlier.
The wrong result you described is one somebody could actually produce on a bad day.
The deliberate breakage was actually run, and the file records what came back rather than what you assumed would.
The failure message would let a colleague locate the problem without asking you what the check meant.
The check still passes on correct work, and you confirmed that rather than assuming it.

If you could not think of a plausible wrong result, that usually means the requirement is still too vague to check against. Go back and make it more specific, because vagueness in the requirement is where the weak check came from in the first place.

lessons.title: Fail cheaply before you mutate
lessons.outcome: Reorder your workflow so cheap fallible checks run before expensive or irreversible steps, and write the outcome scenario that says whose situation this is and what evidence would close it.
lessons.exercise: Write out your workflow as it runs today, score each step for how likely it is to fail and how costly or irreversible it is, then reorder so the cheap fallible checks run first and the irreversible work is gated behind them. Write the outcome scenario above the task list. Run the reordered version once with every side effect simulated, writing to a copy or a draft that nobody depends on.

artifact.description: The workflow in its current order and its reordered form, with the failure likelihood and cost recorded for every step and a reason given for each move, alongside outcome-scenario.md holding the situation, the outcome criteria, the validation evidence and only then the implementation tasks.

verification: Every step carries a note on how likely it is to fail and what it costs if it does.
The first irreversible step in the new order has every cheap check sitting in front of it.
A snapshot step exists before anything is changed, and it names what would be restored.
The scenario states a person's situation and outcome criteria before it lists any task.
The rehearsal run used a copy, a draft or a sandbox, and the file says which.
sourceNotes: Front-Load the Checks That Can Fail.md
The Type System Is the Recovery Oracle for a Dead Agent.md

content.text: Order the steps by what a failure costs

Sort every step in your workflow along two axes: how likely it is to fail, and how expensive or irreversible it is. Then put the cheap, fallible, reversible checks at the front, and gate the expensive or irreversible work behind them.

The anti-pattern is the obvious order, which is to do things in the sequence you happen to think of them. You book the room, order the catering, send the invitations, and then discover that the figures you were going to present will not be signed off until the following week. The check that would have caught it took one message and it ran last.

The question to ask of every step is short. If this fails, what have I already paid for? Anything that can fail cheaply belongs in front of anything that costs real time or cannot be undone. Fetch early, fail fast, and let the expensive ceremony begin only once the fragile parts have passed.
Preflight, snapshot, then change anything

Three phases, in this order. Preflight is everything you can verify without changing anything: the inputs exist, the approvals are in place, the figures are signed off, the recipient list is current. Snapshot is capturing the present state so you can get back to it. Only after both of those does anything get created, sent, filed or paid.

For the whole of this course, keep the last phase simulated or genuinely low risk. Write to a draft, a copy, or a folder nobody depends on. You will be testing your failure paths deliberately in a later lesson, and the first test of a recovery step should not be on something a colleague is relying on.

The snapshot deserves more thought than it usually gets. Write down what it captures and what restoring it would actually involve, in enough detail that somebody else could do it. A snapshot you have never restored from is a hope rather than a step.
State the situation before the tasks

A task list can be completed in full while the situation that prompted it is entirely unchanged. That is the most common way careful work ends up producing nothing, and the fix is to write the situation above the tasks rather than under them.

The scenario has four parts and they go in order. The situation: who is trying to do what, described from their side rather than yours. The outcome criteria: given this situation, when this happens, then this must be true. The validation evidence: what would actually show each criterion was met. Then, last, the implementation tasks, which exist to serve the criteria above them.

Close the scenario when the evidence satisfies the criteria, not when the tasks are ticked off. The lightest form of validation is a person who owns the outcome reading the evidence against the criteria, and that alone is enough to start with. A repeatable check is better where one is possible, and whatever the system tells you afterwards is better still, but neither is a reason to delay using the first.
Building to find out, without the sprawl

Sometimes the quickest way to settle a disagreement is to build a rough version and look at it. That is a legitimate move and it often beats another meeting, particularly now that producing a first version is cheap.

The risk is a run of quick artefacts that each answered a question and together form something incoherent that nobody designed. Making implementation cheaper does not make coherence, reliability or judgement cheaper, and those are the things that decide whether the result is any good.

So bound it before you start. Write the question you are answering, write what result would settle it, and give yourself a limit. If the answer comes back no, throw the artefact away rather than keeping it because it exists. An exploration that quietly becomes a deliverable is how sprawl starts.
What you will make
workflow-before-after.md, with the current order, the reordered version, and a reason for every move.
A failure likelihood and a cost note against each step, however rough.
outcome-scenario.md, holding situation, outcome criteria, validation evidence, and then tasks.
A short record of one rehearsal run with the side effects simulated, naming what the new order caught.
Try it on your work
Write your workflow as a numbered list of steps in the order you currently do them. Include the steps you do without thinking.
Against each step, note how often it goes wrong and what it costs when it does. Rough words are fine: rarely, sometimes, often; cheap, costly, cannot be undone.
Find the first step in your current order that cannot be undone. Everything cheap and fallible should sit in front of it. Move whatever does not.
Add a snapshot step immediately before the first irreversible one, and write down what restoring it would involve.
Write the scenario above the task list: whose situation, what has to become true, and what evidence would show it.
Run the reordered workflow once end to end with every side effect simulated. Send nothing, file nothing, pay nothing.
Record what the new order caught that the old one would have caught late, or record honestly that this run caught nothing.
Check your work
Every step has a note on failure likelihood and on cost, even where the note is a single word.
Nothing cheap and fallible sits after the first irreversible step.
The snapshot step names what it captures and what restoring it would involve.
The scenario describes a person's situation before it lists a single task.
Each outcome criterion has a piece of evidence beside it that would show it was met.
The rehearsal touched only a copy, a draft or a sandbox, and the record says which.
Any exploratory work you did carries the question it was answering and what you decided to do with the result.

technicalExtension.title: Optional lab: use the build as your recovery oracle
technicalExtension.outcome: Recover from an agent that died mid change by compiling everything rather than reading its unfinished narrative, and shape the code so an interrupted write leaves a bounded discoverable mess instead of a silent one.
sourceNotes: The Type System Is the Recovery Oracle for a Dead Agent.md

content.text: Why this is optional

Nothing in the core path assumes a compiler. This lab is for people running autonomous agents against a codebase, where the interesting failure is not a wrong answer but a half-finished write. The next section does not depend on it.
Do not read the narrative, compile

An agent drops mid response. It had already updated a shared enum with new fields but died before reconciling everything that referenced it: its own protocol tests still constructed the old shape, and the matching client methods were never written. The instinct is to read back through its half-finished prose and reconstruct what it meant to do. Do not. The build has already computed the difference between intent and reality, and it will point at exact lines.
There is a trap in the quick version of this check. A library build can pass while the test code is still broken, so a fast build gives you a false all clear. Compile the tests too.

# a library-only build can pass while test code is still broken
cargo build
cargo test --workspace

# same idea elsewhere: type check everything, tests included
tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json
The recovery rule
Treat the type or enum definition as the source of truth. The agent got that far deliberately, so trust it.
Reconcile everything that references it: tests, constructors, call sites, fixtures, until they match.
Run the full test build rather than the library build, because library-only compilation hides breaks in test code and downstream packages.
Shape the code so this stays cheap

This is a quiet argument for strong types and exhaustive matches wherever you let agents write code. When the type system knows a lot, an interrupted write leaves a bounded, enumerable mess. When it knows little, the same interruption leaves a landmine that compiles. Prefer sum types over stringly typed dispatch, and exhaustive matches over a catch-all arm, so that a forgotten variant fails the build rather than slipping through as a default.

It is the same instinct as instrumenting a problem before theorising about it. Gather the evidence first, then reason. Here the compiler is the instrument, and its error list is the evidence you read before reconstructing anybody's intent.

sections.title: Make consequential work inspectable
sections.outcome: Close the points where your workflow could answer from fluent language alone, put a source beside every consequential claim, and leave a record another person can replay without asking you what happened.

lessons.title: Stop the system from guessing
lessons.outcome: Find the points where your workflow could produce an answer from fluent language alone, put privacy and scope filters ahead of the model, and require a source beside every consequential claim.
lessons.exercise: Walk your workflow and mark every point where an answer could be produced without any specific input having been read. For each one, decide what evidence must be fetched first, what filter belongs ahead of the model rather than inside its instructions, and what the workflow does when the evidence is not there.
